# Vāseṭṭha Sutta (Snp 3.9 (PTS Snp 115))

**ID:** Snp 3.9 (PTS Snp 115)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vāseṭṭha Sutta* (Snp 3.9, PTS Snp 115) is the ninth discourse of the Mahāvagga in the *Suttanipāta* [Anderson & Smith 1913]. Set in the Icchānaṅgala forest glade, the discourse opens in prose when two young brāhmaṇas, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, debate whether one is a true brāhmaṇa by birth (*jāti*) or by deeds and action (*kamma*), eventually bringing their dispute to the Buddha [Anderson & Smith 1913; Katre 1931; Collins 1993]. Comprising a prose narrative followed by 63 stanzas—forming the longest poetic ballad outside the *Pārāyanavagga* [Katre 1931]—the Buddha refutes hereditary caste hierarchy by appealing to biological taxonomy: whereas different species of plants, insects, quadrupeds, serpents, and fish possess distinct innate physical differences by birth, human beings share a uniform anatomy and lack fixed biological caste markers [Rahula 1956; Obeyesekere 2002; Chen 2014]. Consequently, caste designations are purely conventional names rooted in social occupation and human habit [Rahula 1956; Obeyesekere 2002]. The discourse culminates in twenty-seven verses that revalue the term "brāhmaṇa" by ethical action, each stanza ending with a refrain defining the genuine holy person through moral purity, non-attachment, and spiritual liberation [Obeyesekere 2002].

Within the Pali canon, the discourse appears almost verbatim as the *Vāseṭṭha Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya* (MN 98) [Rahula 1956; Winternitz 1933; McTighe 2001], a cross-collection duplication supported by DharmaNexus text-reuse data showing near-complete segment alignment (§4.4–69.2 ↔ MN 98 §5.4–14.2) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, the Buddha's verses describing the true brāhmaṇa correspond extensively to the *Brāhmaṇavagga* of the *Dhammapada* (Dhp 396–423) [DharmaNexus]. Parallels and shared verse materials are widely preserved across northern Buddhist canons, including the Sanskrit and Gāndhārī *Dharmapada* and *Udānavarga* traditions (UV 33, G-Dhp 1–50, Patna Dhp) and Chinese Āgama collections (T 210, T 212, T 213, and T 1) [DharmaNexus]. The two protagonists Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja also appear in the *Tevijja Sutta* (DN 13) and *Aggañña Sutta* (DN 27), forming a sequential narrative recognized in Pali commentary tracing their path from initial inquiry to monastic ordination [Collins 1993].
